content.text:
1) Answer

Short version: There is direct evidence, from Nigel Farage’s own platform and public testimony, that he says he wants to protect and strengthen certain human rights—especially freedom of expression, privacy and limits on state surveillance—albeit within a domestic, citizenship‑centred framework rather than through international human‑rights treaties.

Key evidence
- He pledges a British Bill of Rights, stating “Our freedoms must be codified and guaranteed,” alongside promises to protect data and privacy and to limit public surveillance. This is set out in Reform UK’s official 2024 “Contract,” signed off by Farage as party leader. ([assets.nationbuilder.com](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/reformuk/pages/253/attachments/original/1718625371/Reform_UK_Our_Contract_with_You.pdf))
- He also commits to a “Comprehensive Free Speech Bill,” including measures against “de‑banking,” “cancel culture,” and political bias in public institutions; the manifesto further promises penalties for universities that undermine free speech. These are framed as protecting core civil liberties. ([assets.nationbuilder.com](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/reformuk/pages/253/attachments/original/1718625371/Reform_UK_Our_Contract_with_You.pdf))
- In sworn testimony at a U.S. House Judiciary Committee hearing on 3 September 2025, he argued that free speech is a foundational right (e.g., “you can say what you like … that’s what free speech is”) and condemned laws he sees as censorious, such as the UK’s Online Safety Act. Multiple reputable outlets carried his remarks and video. ([news.sky.com](https://news.sky.com/video/nigel-farage-speaks-before-us-congress-on-free-speech-in-the-uk-13424442?utm_source=openai))

Important context (to avoid overclaiming): Farage simultaneously advocates leaving the European Convention on Human Rights and reforming the Human Rights Act “so that it puts the rights of law‑abiding people first”—positions that narrow the scope or venue of rights protection (e.g., fewer rights for non‑citizens, preference for domestic over international enforcement). This shows he promotes a nationally framed set of rights more than a universalist, treaty‑based model; but it does not negate the documentary evidence that he says he wants to protect specific human rights (notably free expression and privacy) for citizens and lawful residents. ([assets.nationbuilder.com](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/reformuk/pages/253/attachments/original/1718625371/Reform_UK_Our_Contract_with_You.pdf))


2) Sources I considered TRUSTWORTHY (with why)

- Source: Reform UK — “Our Contract with You” (official manifesto PDF)
  Reasoning 1 (general): Primary party document; authoritative for the party’s stated policies and priorities.
  Reasoning 2 (for this prompt): It directly records Farage’s platform in his own organisation’s words (Bill of Rights, free‑speech bill, privacy/surveillance limits). ([assets.nationbuilder.com](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/reformuk/pages/253/attachments/original/1718625371/Reform_UK_Our_Contract_with_You.pdf))

- Source: Sky News (video reports of Farage’s 3 Sept 2025 testimony)
  Reasoning 1 (general): Major UK broadcaster with standard editorial processes and on‑the‑record video.
  Reasoning 2 (for this prompt): Provides primary‑style audiovisual evidence of Farage’s free‑speech framing and statements under oath, with time, place and context. ([news.sky.com](https://news.sky.com/video/nigel-farage-speaks-before-us-congress-on-free-speech-in-the-uk-13424442?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Politico (report on the same congressional hearing)
  Reasoning 1 (general): Reputable politics outlet with professional reporting standards; widely cited across parties.
  Reasoning 2 (for this prompt): Corroborates the substance and context of Farage’s testimony and positions on speech regulation. ([politico.com](https://www.politico.com/news/2025/09/03/in-congress-uks-nigel-farage-attacks-his-own-government-on-tech-rules-00541350?utm_source=openai))

- Source: TIME (report on the hearing)
  Reasoning 1 (general): Long‑standing, internationally recognised news magazine with fact‑checking.
  Reasoning 2 (for this prompt): Independent corroboration of what Farage argued and how he framed rights (free speech) at the hearing. ([time.com](https://time.com/7314225/nigel-farage-congress-hearing-trump-relationship-free-speech/?utm_source=openai))


3) Sources I considered NOT TRUSTWORTHY for establishing claims here (and why)

- Source: Dailymotion video reposts (various channels)
  Reasoning 1 (general): Hosting platform; videos can be clipped, re‑uploaded or titled sensationally by third parties; not original reporting.
  Reasoning 2 (for this prompt): I relied instead on primary/official or mainstream original coverage for Farage’s remarks; the reposts weren’t necessary to substantiate claims. ([dailymotion.com](https://www.dailymotion.com/video/x9px9w8?utm_source=openai))

- Source: RealClearPolitics clip page
  Reasoning 1 (general): Aggregator that often embeds third‑party clips and social posts; not itself a primary source for what was said.
  Reasoning 2 (for this prompt): I preferred original broadcaster footage and mainstream reporting to avoid any context loss. ([realclearpolitics.com](https://www.realclearpolitics.com/video/2025/09/03/uk_mp_nigel_farage_responds_to_criticism_from_rep_raskin_you_can_say_what_you_like_thats_what_free_speech_is.html?utm_source=openai))

Notes on scope: I did not rely on Wikipedia or partisan commentary to “prove” the claim; where I opened such pages during research, I cross‑checked any useful lead with primary documents or mainstream reporting and cited those instead.
